images.text:
Vanessa: Amy, I'm sorry I'm pressed for time today.
Amy: That's OK. We have lots of time. We won't run out of time, so take your time.
Vanessa: I had a terrible day at work yesterday. I really think I'm starting to lose it.
Amy: What happened?
Vanessa: I had some people quit on me. I was just trying to establish some orderliness and they thought my demands were unreasonable. So in the last two days, I have canned a supplier and had three employees quit. It's been an appalling week so far. Perhaps I'm too strict?
Amy: If you hadn't created rules, there would have been no discipline. Had people quit before?
Vanessa: Sure. Just not so hysterically.
Amy: I'm curious Vanessa. What was your background before you started this job?
Vanessa: I was a chef. I studied at the Blue Ribbon Institute in San Francisco. If I hadn't studied there, I probably would have never gotten into the restaurant business. Also, if I hadn't gone out to the west coast, I would have never seen how beautiful California is. Have you been?
Amy: No.

Vanessa: It's gorgeous. I lived in San Francisco for nine months before I got homesick and came back to Boston.
Amy: Are you from here?
Vanessa: No, the UK. I settled here after school.
Amy: How long did you work as a sous-chef?
Vanessa: Six months. I would have gotten really good, if I had worked as sous-chef a little longer.
Amy: Did you enjoy it?
Vanessa: I had a great time there. I really liked San Francisco too, but it's too far. If my friends had lived somewhere closer, I would have stayed out there.

Amy: Have you ever wondered what your life would have been like if you had stayed in San Francisco? Have you ever wondered what your life would have been like if you had remained a sous-chef? My point is, I wonder if managing is truly making you happy. Maybe you should take some time away?
Vanessa: I don't know. I guess I have been under a lot of pressure lately and that's why I'm thinking the way I am.
Amy: Are you burning out?
Vanessa: Maybe. I sometimes wonder if I have worked too much this past year. I suppose I have burned the candle at both ends for a little long now.
Amy: Vanessa, do the life balance wheel for me.

When you talk about the unreal past, you express things that did not happen in reality in the past. You use past tenses to talk about unreal situations.

You use the Type 3 Conditional to express conditions in the past that did not happen or to express criticism or regret with would have, could have or should have.

Structure:
If + subject + Past Perfect, subject + Perfect Conditional

Example:
If my employees had studied at the Blue Ribbon, they wouldn't have quit so easily.
The condition of having studied at the Blue Ribbon is unreal. As a result, they have quit too easily.
If you hadn't created rules, there would have been no discipline.
If I hadn't studied there, I probably would have never gotten into the restaurant business.
Also, if I hadn't gone out to the west coast, I would have never seen how beautiful California is.
I would have gotten really good if I had worked as a sous-chef a little longer.
If my friends had lived somewhere closer, I would have stayed out there.
Colloquial expressions are idioms that you use frequently, especially in spoken English. There are many expressions that refer to time in English.

Colloquial expressions about time can refer to different aspects of time.
Here are some colloquial expressions:

Lack of time:
pressed for time
run out of time

Have enough time:
lots of time
take your time

The right time for something:
a great time
I had a great time there.
I'm sorry I'm pressed for time today.
That's OK. We have lots of time.
We won't run out of time, so take your time.
